On August 19, 2004, Google became a [public company](/wiki/Public_company "Public company") via an initial public offering. At that time Page, Brin and Schmidt agreed to work together at Google for 20 years, until the year 2024.[[69]](#cite_note-70) The company opened on the [NASDAQ National Market](/wiki/NASDAQ_National_Market "NASDAQ National Market") under the five-letter ticker symbol GOOGL with an offering of 19,605,052 shares at a price of $85 per share.[[70]](#cite_note-IPO-71)[[71]](#cite_note-GoogleAnnualReport2004-72) Shares were sold in an online auction format using a system built by [Morgan Stanley](/wiki/Morgan_Stanley "Morgan Stanley") and [Credit Suisse](/wiki/Credit_Suisse "Credit Suisse"), underwriters for the deal.[[72]](#cite_note-73)[[73]](#cite_note-74) The sale of $1.67 billion gave Google a [market capitalization](/wiki/Market_capitalization "Market capitalization") of more than $23 billion.[[74]](#cite_note-washpost-75)

On October 9, 2006, Google acquired [YouTube](/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") for $1.65 billion in Google stock.[[75]](#cite_note-76)[[76]](#cite_note-77)[[77]](#cite_note-78)[[78]](#cite_note-79) On July 20, 2007, Google bid $4.6 billion for the wireless-spectrum auction by the [FCC](/wiki/FCC "FCC").[[79]](#cite_note-80) On March 11, 2008, Google acquired [DoubleClick](/wiki/DoubleClick "DoubleClick") for $3.1 billion, transferring to Google valuable relationships that DoubleClick had with Web publishers and advertising agencies.[[80]](#cite_note-81)[[81]](#cite_note-82) By 2011, Google was handling approximately 3 billion searches per

Further information: [Music of England](/wiki/Music_of_England_(disambiguation) "Music of England (disambiguation)"), [Music of Scotland](/wiki/Music_of_Scotland "Music of Scotland"), [Music of Wales](/wiki/Music_of_Wales "Music of Wales"), and [Music of Northern Ireland](/wiki/Music_of_Northern_Ireland "Music of Northern Ireland")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Royal_Albert_Hall%2C_BBC_Proms_2017.jpg/250px-Royal_Albert_Hall%2C_BBC_Proms_2017.jpg)](/wiki/File:Royal_Albert_Hall,_BBC_Proms_2017.jpg)

[The Proms](/wiki/The_Proms "The Proms") is a classical music festival, most closely associated with [Henry Wood](/wiki/Henry_Wood "Henry Wood") and held at the [Royal Albert Hall](/wiki/Royal_Albert_Hall "Royal Albert Hall") in London, which regularly plays music by [Edward Elgar](/wiki/Edward_Elgar "Edward Elgar") and other British composers.

Various styles of music have become popular in the UK, including the [folk music](/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music") of [England](/wiki/Folk_music_of_England "Folk music of England"), [Scotland](/wiki/Folk_music_of_Scotland "Folk music of Scotland"), [Wales](/wiki/Music_of_Wales#Folk_music "Music of Wales") and [Northern Ireland](/wiki/Folk_music_of_Northern_Ireland "Folk music of Northern Ireland"). English folk features melodic ballads with strong lyrics and music for country dancing often using accordion and fiddles.[[466]](#cite_note-488) Scottish folk features bagpipes and fiddles playing traditional dance tunes with bouncy tempos.[[467]](#cite_note-489) Welsh folk has harps and vocal harmonies often sung in Welsh.[[468]](#cite_note-490) Northern Irish folk blends fiddles with flutes merging Scottish and Irish influences.[[469]](#cite_note-491)

Historically, there has been [Renaissance music](/wiki/Renaissance_music "Renaissance music"

Main article: [Liu Chuanzhi](/wiki/Liu_Chuanzhi "Liu Chuanzhi")

Liu Chuanzhi is the founder and former chairman of Lenovo. Liu was trained as an engineer at a military college and later went on to work at the [Chinese Academy of Sciences](/wiki/Chinese_Academy_of_Sciences "Chinese Academy of Sciences"). Like many young people during the Cultural Revolution, Liu was denounced and sent to the countryside where he worked as a laborer on a rice farm. Liu claims [Hewlett-Packard](/wiki/Hewlett-Packard "Hewlett-Packard") as a key source of inspiration. In an interview with *[The Economist](/wiki/The_Economist "The Economist")* he stated that "Our earliest and best teacher was Hewlett-Packard." For more than ten years, Lenovo was Hewlett-Packard's distributor in China.[[201]](#cite_note-Economist-201) In reference to Lenovo's later acquisition of IBM's personal computer unit Liu said, "I remember the first time I took part in a meeting of IBM agents. I was wearing an old business suit of my father's and I sat in the back row. Even in my dreams, I never imagined that one day we could buy the IBM PC business. It was unthinkable. Impossible."[[27]](#cite_note-chief-27)

In 2016, *[Harry Potter and the Cursed Child](/wiki/Harry_Potter_and_the_Cursed_Child "Harry Potter and the Cursed Child")* was released, a two-part play written by [Jack Thorne](/wiki/Jack_Thorne "Jack Thorne") based on an original story by Rowling, Thorne, and [John Tiffany](/wiki/John_Tiffany "John Tiffany").[[122]](#cite_note-124) Billed as the eighth story in the *Harry Potter* series, it picks up where the epilogue of *Deathly Hallows* left off, following an adult Harry Potter and his son, [Albus Severus Potter](/wiki/Albus_Severus_Potter "Albus Severus Potter").[[123]](#cite_note-125) Previews of the play began at the [Palace Theatre, London](/wiki/Palace_Theatre,_London "Palace Theatre, London"), on 7 June 2016,[[124]](#cite_note-nyt07june2016-126) and it premiered on 30 July 2016. The play opened on Broadway on 21 April 2018 at the [Lyric Theatre](/wiki/Lyric_Theatre_(New_York_City,_1998) "Lyric Theatre (New York City, 1998)"), with previews starting on 16 March 2018. Both parts of the stage play's script have been released in print and digital formats as *Harry Potter and the Cursed Child Parts I & II*. The first edition, the Special Rehearsal Edition, corresponded to the script used in the preview shows and was published on 31 July 2016, the date of Harry's birthday in the series and Rowling's birthday, as well. Since revisions to the script continued after the book was printed, an edited version was released on 25 July 2017, as the "Definitive Collector's Edition". According to CNN, this was the most preordered book of 2016.[[125]](#cite_note-127)

Main article: [Gravity of Earth](/wiki/Gravity_of_Earth "Gravity of Earth")

The gravity of Earth is the [acceleration](/wiki/Acceleration "Acceleration") that is imparted to objects due to the distribution of mass within Earth. Near Earth's surface, [gravitational acceleration](/wiki/Gravitational_acceleration "Gravitational acceleration") is approximately 9.8 m/s2 (32 ft/s2). Local differences in topography, geology, and deeper tectonic structure cause local and broad regional differences in Earth's gravitational field, known as [gravity anomalies](/wiki/Gravity_anomaly "Gravity anomaly").[[199]](#cite_note-210) The [Hill sphere](/wiki/Hill_sphere "Hill sphere"), or the [sphere of gravitational influence](/wiki/Sphere_of_influence_(astrodynamics) "Sphere of influence (astrodynamics)"), of Earth is about 1.5 million km (930,000 mi) in radius.[[200]](#cite_note-vazquez_etal2006-211)[[n 12]](#cite_note-hill_radius-212) This is the maximum distance at which Earth's gravitational influence is stronger than that of the more distant Sun and planets. Objects must orbit Earth within this radius, or they can become unbound by the gravitational perturbation of the Sun.[[200]](#cite_note-vazquez_etal2006-211)

In [Allied countries](/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") during the war, the "Pacific War" was not usually distinguished from [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), or was known simply as the *War against Japan*. In the United States, the term *[Pacific theater](/wiki/Asiatic-Pacific_theater "Asiatic-Pacific theater")* was widely used. The [US Armed Forces](/wiki/US_Armed_Forces "US Armed Forces") considered the [China Burma India theater](/wiki/China_Burma_India_theater "China Burma India theater") to be distinct from the [Asiatic-Pacific theater](/wiki/Asiatic-Pacific_theater "Asiatic-Pacific theater") during the conflict.[[41]](#cite_note-49)

Japan used the name *Greater East Asia War* (大東亜戦争, *Dai Tō-A Sensō*), as chosen by a cabinet decision on 10 December 1941, to refer to both the war with the Western Allies and the ongoing war in China. This name was released to the public on 12 December, with an explanation that it involved [Asian](/wiki/Asia "Asia") nations achieving their independence from the Western powers through armed forces of the [Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere](/wiki/Greater_East_Asia_Co-Prosperity_Sphere "Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere").[[42]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJansen2002626-50) Japanese officials integrated what they called the *Japan–China Incident* (日支事変, *Nisshi Jihen*) into the Greater East Asia War. During the [Occupation of Japan](/wiki/Occupation_of_Japan "Occupation of Japan") (1945–1952), these terms were prohibited in official documents (although their informal usage continued). The war became officially known as the Pacific War (太平洋戦争, *Taiheiyō Sensō*). The *Fifteen Years' War* (十五年戦争, *Jūgonen Sensō*) is also used, referring to the period from the [Mukden incident](/wiki/Mukden_incident "Mukden incident") of 1931 through 1945.[[43]](#cite_note-51)

The first focus on issues of grade inflation by the Princeton administration began in 1998 when a university report was released showcasing a steady rise in undergraduate grades from 1973 to 1997.[[258]](#cite_note-Princetonian-2004-261)[[259]](#cite_note-Foderaro-2010-262) Subsequent reports and discussion from the report culminated to when in 2004,[[258]](#cite_note-Princetonian-2004-261) [Nancy Weiss Malkiel](/wiki/Nancy_Weiss_Malkiel "Nancy Weiss Malkiel"), the dean of the college, implemented a grade deflation policy to address the findings.[[260]](#cite_note-On_grade_deflation-263) Malkiel's reason for the policy was that an A was becoming devalued as a larger percentage of the student body received one.[[260]](#cite_note-On_grade_deflation-263) Following its introduction, the number of A's and average GPA on campus dropped, although A's and B's were still the most frequent grades awarded.[[259]](#cite_note-Foderaro-2010-262)[[261]](#cite_note-264) The policy received mixed approval from both faculty and students when first instituted.[[258]](#cite_note-Princetonian-2004-261)[[262]](#cite_note-265) Criticism for grade deflation continued through the years, with students alleging negative effects like increased competition and lack of willingness to choose challenging classes.[[260]](#cite_note-On_grade_deflation-263)[[263]](#cite_note-266) Other criticism included job market and graduate school prospects, although Malkiel responded by saying that she sent 3,000 letters to numerous institutions and employers informing them.[[259]](#cite_note-Foderaro-2010-262)[[260]](#cite_note-On_grade_deflation-263) In 2009, transcripts began including a statement about the policy.[[264]](#cite_note-Levenson-2013-267)

In October 2013, Princeton President Christopher Eisgruber created a faculty committee to review the deflation policy.[[264]](#cite_note-Levenson-2013-267) In August 2014

**Jorge Mario Pedro Vargas Llosa,[[a]](#cite_note-1)[[b]](#cite_note-2) 1st Marquess of Vargas Llosa** (28 March 1936 – 13 April 2025) was a Peruvian novelist, journalist, essayist, and politician. Vargas Llosa was one of the most significant Latin American novelists and essayists and one of the leading writers of his generation. Some critics consider him to have had a more substantial international impact and worldwide audience than any other writer of the [Latin American Boom](/wiki/Latin_American_Boom "Latin American Boom"). [In 2010](/wiki/2010_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "2010 Nobel Prize in Literature"), he won the [Nobel Prize in Literature](/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature") for "his cartography of structures of power and his trenchant images of the individual's resistance, revolt, and defeat".

Amin H. Nasser :: Career :: chunk_0001
Nasser began his career with Saudi Aramco in 1982 as an engineer in the oil production department and proceeded to work in drilling and reservoir management. In 1997, he became manager of the [Ras Tanura](/wiki/Ras_Tanura "Ras Tanura") Producing Department. Later he became manager of the Northern Area Production Engineering Department, as well as the [Safaniya](/wiki/Safaniya_Oil_Field "Safaniya Oil Field") Aramco.com Offshore and Onshore Producing Departments.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He was appointed Chief Petroleum Engineer in 2004. He was cited as the company's vice president for petroleum engineering and development in 2007.[[6]](#cite_note-6) He became Senior Vice President of Saudi Aramco's Upstream operations in 2008.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Nasser became acting President and CEO of Aramco in May 2015, and was made permanent in September 2015.[[1]](#cite_note-:1-1)

As CEO, he led the company's response to drone and missile attacks on its facilities in September 2019.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Prior to Aramco's initial public offering (IPO), he led the company's entry into the global debt and capital markets with its first bond issuance.[[9]](#cite_note-9) He oversaw Aramco's 2019 IPO in which it became the world's most valuable listed company, and led its 2020 acquisition of Saudi petrochemicals giant [SABIC](/wiki/SABIC "SABIC").[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)

In 2021, amid growing pressure for fossil fuel companies to become greener to contribute to [climate change mitigation](/wiki/Climate_change_mitigation "Climate change mitigation"), Nasser warned countries against divesting in [fossil fuels](/wiki/Fossil_fuels "Fossil fuels"), arguing that it would cause inflation and unrest.[[2]](#cite_note-:2-2)

Breast cancer :: Prognosis :: chunk_0011
Different countries have different prognoses. In the United States, the UK, South Korea, Japan, and Australia, more than 90% of women survive breast cancer for at least five years from diagnosis. In China, this is 82%.[[90]](#cite_note-Tao2023-90)[[16]](#cite_note-CRUK-16) India saw a 66% survival rate.[[5]](#cite_note-Sathishkumar2024-5)

Breast cancer prognosis varies widely depending on how far the tumor has spread at the time of diagnosis. Overall, 92% of women diagnosed with breast cancer in the United States [survive at least five years](/wiki/Five-year_survival_rate "Five-year survival rate") from diagnosis. Those whose tumor(s) are completely confined to the breast (nearly two-thirds of cases) have the best prognoses – 100% survive at least five years. Those whose tumors have metastasized to distant sites have relatively poor prognoses – 33% survive at least five years from the time of diagnosis.[[4]](#cite_note-SEER2026-4)

Triple-negative breast cancer (up to 15% of cases) and inflammatory breast cancer (up to 5% of cases) are particularly aggressive and have relatively poor prognoses.[[91]](#cite_note-ACS-TNBC-91)[[92]](#cite_note-ACS-IBC-92) Those with triple-negative breast cancer have an overall five-year survival rate of 78% – 92% for those whose tumors are confined to the breast; 15% for those with metastases.[[91]](#cite_note-ACS-TNBC-91) Those with inflammatory breast cancer are diagnosed after the cancer has already spread to the skin of the breast. They have an overall five-year survival rate of 40%; 22% for those with metastases.[[92]](#cite_note-ACS-IBC-92) The relatively rare tumors with tubular, mucinous, or medullary growth tend to have better prognoses.[[93]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHayesLippman2022"Prognostic_Factors"-93)
